title: The role of radiographic knee alignment in total knee replacement outcomes and opportunities for artificial intelligence-driven assessment

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《The role of radiographic knee alignment in total knee replacement outcomes and opportunities for artificial intelligence-driven assessment》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Introduction · p0025】This review article aims to: i) Explore possible radiographic knee alignment biomarkers for TKR outcomes and relevant techniques for their assessment. ii) Investigate and summarise the current literature on AI-based techniques used to assess radiographic knee alignment for TKR outcomes. iii) Discuss available commercial products for automated knee alignment measurement. iv) Identify gaps and possible future directions for generating automated knee alignment biomarkers for TKR outcomes and predictions of TKR outcomes.

【Introduction · p0010】Knee osteoarthritis (OA) is one of the most widespread and burdensome health problems [1], [2], [3], [4]. Total knee replacement (TKR) may be offered as treatment for end-stage knee OA. Nevertheless, TKR is an invasive procedure involving prosthesis implantation at the knee joint, and around 10% of patients are dissatisfied following TKR [5], [6]. Dissatisfaction is often assessed through patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) [7]. In clinical practice, predicting poor TKR outcomes in advance could help optimise patient selection and improve management strategies.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《The role of radiographic knee alignment in total knee replacement outcomes and opportunities for artificial intelligence-driven assessment》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) scoring protocols for TKR · p0030】Specific scoring protocols are used to pre- and postoperatively collect PROMs in TKR patients. These protocols are important to TKR outcome evaluation and prediction. They can indicate if a patient’s OA status negatively affects their quality of life in terms of both pain and function. However, these instruments differ in purpose. Some were developed specifically for assessing outcomes after knee arthroplasty, whereas others were originally designed for knee osteoarthritis (OA) assessment and were later applied to TKR cohorts. Therefore, their suitability depends on whether the aim is to assess preoperative OA severity, postoperative recovery, or change in symptoms and function after surgery.

【Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) scoring protocols for TKR · p0035】The Knee Society Score [23] is a knee arthroplasty-specific outcome measure that combines clinician-assessed evaluation of pain, range of motion, stability, and alignment with assessment of functional activities such as walking and stair climbing, and it has been widely used to assess patients before and after TKR. The Oxford Knee Score (OKS) [24] is a 12-item patient-reported outcome measure specifically developed to assess pain and function after TKR and is commonly administered both preoperatively and postoperatively to quantify surgical outcome. In contrast, the Knee Injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) [25] and the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) [26] are broader knee OA instruments. KOOS was developed to assess symptoms, pain, activities of daily living, sport/recreation, and knee-related quality of life in patients with knee injury or OA, and it has also been validated for use in total knee replacement populations. WOMAC was originally developed for patients with hip or knee OA and evaluates pain, stiffness, and physical function; it is therefore particularly suitable for assessing OA-related disease burden before TKR, but it has also been used to evaluate postoperative changes after TKR. An overview of these scoring systems is listed in Table 1.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《The role of radiographic knee alignment in total knee replacement outcomes and opportunities for artificial intelligence-driven assessment》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Discussions and conclusions · p0140】Knee alignment is associated with TKR outcomes: varus and valgus deformities may predict greater postoperative improvement [27] but also increased revision risk [9], while postoperative malalignment is associated with long-term component failure [31]. However, no clear relationship was found between knee alignment and postoperative outcomes when assessed using OKS [32], warranting evaluation using additional outcome measures.

【Discussions and conclusions · p0150】AI-based techniques could provide accurate and efficient knee alignment assessments. Many approaches showed excellent accuracy comparable to manual measurements [10], [11], [13], [85], [88]. Some angles, such as HKAA, traditionally require full-leg radiographs. However, acquiring and pre-processing these images can be time-consuming, and they result in increased radiation exposure. Therefore, predicting these measurements from standard weight-bearing knee radiographs would be clinically valuable. Current HKAA prediction approaches from standard weight-bearing knee radiographs remain unstable, highlighting the need for more robust and reliable models [33]. Most existing alignment assessments methods rely on landmark detection, though direct angle prediction could provide an alternative pathway [10], [33]. Furthermore, many studies lack radiologist-provided manual annotations or independent validation, limiting confidence in generalisability [10], [33]. Future work should emphasise external validation on unseen data to demonstrate clinical applicability and reliable performance across practice settings.

AI-based techniques could provide accurate and efficient knee alignment assessments. Many approaches showed excellent accuracy comparable to manual measurements [10], [11], [13], [85], [88]. Some angles, such as HKAA, traditionally require full-leg radiographs. However, acquiring and pre-processing these images can be time-consuming, and they result in increased radiation exposure. Therefore, predicting these measurements from standard weight-bearing knee radiographs would be clinically valuable. Current HKAA prediction approaches from standard weight-bearing knee radiographs remain unstable, highlighting the need for more robust and reliable models [33]. Most existing alignment assessments methods rely on landmark detection, though direct angle prediction could provide an alternative pathway [10], [33]. Furthermore, many studies lack radiologist-provided manual annotations or independent validation, limiting confidence in generalisability [10], [33]. Future work should emphasise external validation on unseen data to demonstrate clinical applicability and reliable performance across practice settings.
